title: Shared Involvement
internal_section_headings: Macro Phase: Socializing in Game Worlds
Governance in Massively Multiplayer On-line Games
Micro Phase: Collaboration, Competition, and Cohabitation during Gameplay
figure_captions: Figure 6.1 — A wedding inside Second Life (Linden Lab, 2003). Image courtesy of Marco Cadioli (a.k.a Marco Manray).
Figure 6.2 — Surrounded by AI characters in Assassin's Creed (Ubisoft Montreal, 2007).

expected_concepts: macro phase: socializing in persistent game worlds (MMOG sociality)
MMOGs as full-fledged on-line societies (friendships, marriages, betrayals)
guilds, end-game content, and prerequisite collaboration
out-of-game friendships and geographically organized guilds
governance in MMOGs / Terms of Use enforcement (Sara Andrews / Blizzard incident)
magic circle critique applied to corporate governance of virtual worlds
MMOGs as 'third places' (Oldenburg) — bridging vs bonding social capital
micro phase: collaboration, competition, and cohabitation during gameplay
human-controlled vs computer-controlled agents (perceptual distinction)
cohabitation as anchoring presence (avatar in living environment)
media equation: treating computers as social actors
persistent reputation in MMOGs (kill-on-sight lists, ninja-looting, ganking)
spectatorship and performance for audience (co-located + remote)
clans, trials, and screening via spectator mode
cooperation: co-op games, LAN gaming, MMOG group/guild structures
designed interdependence (Left 4 Dead AI director mechanics)
competition (agon, Caillois) and globally distributed real-time contests
social contingency (Malaby) codependent on performative contingency
AI agent limitations: pinpoint FPS accuracy vs lack of holistic awareness
shift from individual to team-play / semiprofessional competitive clans
internalization of shared involvement (conscious to mastery)

phase2_special_guidance: Dimension-chapter template (see plan §5). Shared is the chapter whose dissertation Layer-C anchor is Mitsein (BCAP), NOT Uexküll — per plan §3.D.i. Per Phase 0 CRITICAL FINDING, confirmed by full-text scan of pp.93–112, Calleja cites NO Heidegger, NO Goffman, NO Husserl, NO Merleau-Ponty in this chapter. All Layer-C edges (Mitsein, Burke-Agent, anticipatory Uexküll) MUST carry provenance='anticipatory-projection (dissertation)'. Layer-A edges may anchor directly in Steinkuehler & Williams, T. L. Taylor, Castronova, Oldenburg, Reeves & Nass, Caillois, Malaby, Lim & Reeves, Rambusch et al., Gerhard et al., Calo, Manninen & Kujanpaa, Heide-Smith. SPECIAL ATTENTION: (1) capture Calleja's distinction between mere co-presence/cohabitation (avatars as ambient density, including with rudimentary AI per Reeves-Nass/Gerhard-Moore-Hobbs) and shared-involvement proper (involving social bond / reputation / interdependence) — this distinction is substantive and load-bearing; (2) flag any 'frame' or performance-for-audience moves (esp. the spectatorship subsection under Cohabitation, and the co-located FIFA-2009 living-room example) as candidates for Burke 'Agent' pentad mapping and anticipatory Goffman bridge; (3) the Sara Andrews / Blizzard governance case study is the longest sustained example in the chapter and should be treated as a primary Layer-A node with multiple edges (magic-circle critique, Terms of Use, server-consensus enforcement, das-Man-anticipatory); (4) note Calleja's enumeration slip at p.101: 'there are four dimensions of shared involvement: cohabitation, competition, and cooperation' — he writes 'four' but lists only three (and only three subsections follow). Treat as authorial typo; do not invent a fourth dimension. Emit ~35 edges weighted toward (a) intra-Calleja scaffold (macro→governance→micro→cohabitation→cooperation→competition), (b) direct citation edges to Steinkuehler-Williams/Taylor/Castronova/Oldenburg/Reeves-Nass/Caillois/Malaby/Rambusch/Lim-Reeves, and (c) anticipatory Layer-C bridges to Mitsein/Burke-Agent/anticipatory-Goffman.
